## Kaccāyanasāra Pāḷi
## Sāmaññaniddesa

1. May that Sun-like Buddha, the Conqueror, who has overcome the five Māras, dispelled the darkness of delusion with the rays of the True Dhamma, and caused the lotus-like multitude of beings to bloom, protect me well.

2. In the Dispensation of the Buddha, for the sake of increasing the wisdom of those who are not yet proficient in the field of grammar, I shall speak the Kaccāyanasāra, the essence of the Kaccāyana treatise, in the Māgadha language, based on the Janghadāsaka treatise composed by the teacher Janghadāsaka.

3. In whatever sense of the agent (kattar) and so forth, the verbal (ākhyāta), kitaka, samāsa, and taddhita occur (as appropriate), the sense of the agent etc. expressed by those (verbs etc.) is called 'vutta' (expressed) in that context. In that expressed sense, the nominative case (paṭhamā) is used because one wishes to indicate only the mere meaning of the stem (liṅgattha).

4. The verbal (ākhyāta) occurs in the sense of the agent and the object (kamma). The taddhita occurs in senses excluding the ablative (avadhi). The kitaka occurs in senses excluding the possessive (sāmī). The samāsa occurs in all senses. (These expressors) occur in both general (sāmañña) and specific (visesa) meanings.

5. Words such as kitaka are called expressors (vācaka). These expressors are subordinate (guṇa) and function only as qualifiers (visesana). The first (the verb) takes a number (saṅkhyā) beyond its own expressed meaning. The remaining (kitaka, samāsa, taddhita) take gender (liṅga) and so forth.
2:
6. If it occurs in a compound sentence (vākya-dvanda) which is a collection of nouns, the numbers of the non-predominant qualifier (visesana) depend on the whole or the parts.

7. In a sentence where both the original state (prakati) and the transformed state (vikati) are mentioned, the expressor (vācaka) takes the number of the original state because that original state is primary (padhāna).

8. The qualifying sense is called visesana (bheda), and the sense to be qualified is called visesya (bhedya). If those two have the same meaning, the qualifier (bhedaka) generally takes the gender and so forth of the qualified (bhedya).

9. The well-known object that establishes an unknown object by way of a similar nature is called upamāna (simile). The unknown object is called upameyya (the object of comparison). These two possess the same case ending (vibhatti).

10. The verbal expressor (ākhyāta-vācaka) is in the second person (majjhima-purisa) whether the word 'tumha' (you) is directly used or understood. Likewise, it is in the first person (uttama-purisa) with the word 'amha' (I/we). With the remaining nouns, it is in the third person (paṭhama-purisa).
3:
11. When expressing the same time and the same action, if nouns and so forth are expressed, among the persons such as the third person (paṭhama) following the root, only the later person occurs.

12. When the words 'tumha' and 'amha' are indicated in the sense of 'abhūtatabbhāva' (becoming what was not), which is the meaning of the suffix 'cī', their respective second and first persons do not occur. The sense that is first taken and then abandoned is called 'upāya'. The sense that is established by that upāya is called 'upeyya'.

13. The original agent (suddha-kattar) of roots meaning going, knowing, eating, or making sound, as well as intransitive roots and roots such as 'bhajja', receives the name 'object' (kamma) when joined with a causative suffix (kārita).

14. The agent of the root 'nī', 'khāda', 'hve' preceded by 'ā', 'ad', the nominal root 'saddāya', and 'kanda' should not receive the name 'object' even when there is a causative suffix. Likewise, the name 'object' should not be applied to the root 'vaha' when there is no causative agent (hetu-kattar) who constantly instigates, nor to the root 'bhakkha' in the sense of non-injury.

15. Among roots such as 'nī' and 'vaha', the primary object is expressed. Among roots such as 'duha', the secondary object is expressed. Among roots joined with a causative suffix, their own causative object (kārita-kamma) is expressed. The causative agent (kārita-kattar) who commands or instigates is also expressed.
4:
16. Due to the absence of its own expressed object, the case ending or suffix in the sense of the object, or the verbal ending expressing the object, must express another object. However, if another object is possible, the verbal ending does not express time (kāla), distance (addha), action (bhāva), or place (desa).

17. The status of being an object for time, distance, action, and place can certainly occur when they are joined with intransitive roots that have another internal action (or where another action is included within).

18. Whatever kāraka (grammatical relation) is expressed by the primary verbs, namely kitaka and ākhyāta, that kāraka appears as if expressed even if it is not expressed by the subordinate qualifying verbs, because the substance (drabya) is not different.

19. A kāraka expressed by expressors such as kitaka may also become 'vutta' (expressed) or 'avutta' (unexpressed) due to other words such as ākhyāta. In some cases, a kāraka not expressed by expressors such as kitaka may become 'avutta' or 'vutta' due to other words.
5:
## Ākhyātaniddesa

20. Parassapada endings occur only in the sense of the agent (kattar). Attanopada endings, however, occur in all three senses: state (bhāva), object (kamma), and agent (kattar). All vikaraṇa suffixes occur in the sense of the agent when a sabbadhātuka ending follows.

21. Among these vikaraṇa suffixes, some are desired to be applied even when an asabbadhātuka ending follows. Endings such as the present (vattamānā) occur in the respective times such as the present (paccuppanna) in order.

22. An action that has started but is not yet finished is called present (paccuppanna). An action that is well finished is called past (atīta). An action that has not yet reached arising but is imminent is called future (anāgata).

23. The status of the parokkhā (perfect) ending should be known in these three cases: when a deficient agent does not remember his own past action, in cases of absolute concealment, and in the absence of direct perception etc.

24. The last watch (yāma) of the past night or half of that watch, and the first watch (paho) of the coming future night or half of that watch, together with the whole day, is called 'today' (ajja) in this context.

25. The non-occurrence of actions due to connection with a contrary cause or due to the deficiency of a suitable cause is called 'kriyātipanna' (conditional).
6:
26. That kriyātipanna is of two kinds: the past, which occurs due to the fulfillment of causes, and the future, which occurs due to seeing some sign or omen.

27. The imperative (pañcamī) and optative (sattamī) endings occur without depending on a specific time. Their domains are stated to be the senses of request (patthanā), injunction (vidhi), and inquiry (sampucchā).

28. Among those senses, longing is called patthanā. Commanding or instigating is called vidhi; that vidhi is of two kinds: respectful instigation and non-respectful commanding. Inquiring as in "Is it thus?" is called sampucchā.

29. When the time of an action is intended, all endings such as the present (vattamānā) occur according to their respective times, and due to being combined with other words,

30. They express other times such as the future after the word has been formed. This example should be known: "purā dibbati asaddhammo" (before the false dhamma spreads).

31. That sense which is known through another word does not negate the sense that arises during the formation of the word. This is because that (external) sense is an external factor (bahiraṅga).

32. This entire establishment of words and meanings exists only according to the intention (vivacchā) of the speaker. The intention is also understood by following the sequence of well-known Pāḷi examples.
7:
## Kitanidessa

33. It has been said that the kicca suffixes occur in the sense of state (bhāva) and in the sense of the object (kamma). Likewise, suffixes having the sense of the kha suffix also occur [in the senses of bhāva and kamma]. In some instances, the kicca suffixes occur in other senses [besides bhāva and kamma]. The yu suffix, however, occurs in all means of accomplishment (sādhana).

34. After roots meaning "making a sound" and roots such as ruca, etc., the [yu suffix] occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar) when senses such as habitual nature (tassīla) are understood. The suffixes ṇī, tu, and āvī also occur in the sense of the agent after all roots when senses such as habitual nature are understood.

35. The ta suffix occurs in the sense of state (bhāva) and in the sense of the object (kamma) in the past tense. It also occurs in the sense of the agent in the past tense after the roots ṭhā, āsa, vasa, the root ruha preceded by ā, jara, sī, janī, silisa, and roots meaning "exertion," as well as after intransitive (akammaka) roots.
8:
36. The ta suffix occurs in the aforementioned senses of state (bhāva), object (kamma), and agent (kattar), and also in the sense of location (ādhāra), after roots meaning "going" (gati), roots meaning "eating or swallowing" (āhāra), and after intransitive roots. However, after roots with an unexpressed object, the ta suffix occurs only in the sense of state (bhāva).

37. After all roots, the suffixes tavantu, ṇvu, tu, and āvī occur in the sense of the agent (kattar). Generally, suffixes such as ṇa occur in the sense of state (bhāva). Among those suffixes, some also occur in the senses of the six relations (kāraka).

38. The state (bhāva) of a primary derivative (kita) is like a substance (dabba). Therefore, relations such as the object (kamma) also occur. Generally, even when an object is present, kita suffixes are prescribed in the sense of state (bhāva).

39. Among preceding and succeeding actions having the same agent, suffixes such as tvā occur after the preceding action in the sense of state (bhāva). The tuṃ suffix occurs in the sense of state (bhāva) when there is an action that is the purpose of the action to which the tuṃ suffix is attached, or when there are actions such as "desiring" (icchā).

40. This sense of state (bhāva) is the sense of the suffix, because it is not manifest without that suffix. In the same way, it is also the sense of the root. Therefore, all senses such as state (bhāva) are the sense of the combination of the root and the suffix.
9:
41. This classification and analysis occur only at the time of learning the conventional language. It should be viewed in this way: "This sense belongs to the original stem or root; this sense belongs to the suffix or inflection."

42. This grammar commonly taught now is considered a mere imitation of the eternal language (nicca saddā). Therefore, in some cases, the mutual accomplishment of the example (lakkha) and the rule (lakkhaṇa) is not prohibited.

43. This light called "sound" or "language" (sadda) is beginningless. If this light is not manifest to someone, it is revealed by the treatise on grammar for their understanding, like revealing a lamp that was covered.

44. The māna and anta suffixes occur in the present tense, in the sense of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and in the sense of cause (hetu). Primary derivative (kita) suffixes also occur in other tenses when connected with the sense of the root.

45. Primary derivative (kita) suffixes follow the gender of the sense they denote. The a suffix occurring after roots ending in i or ī (ivaṇṇa), roots ending in u or ū (uvaṇṇa), and roots such as vara, as well as the second ṇa suffix and the i suffix, occur in the masculine gender.

46. The yu suffix in senses other than the agent (akattar), and the kicca and ta suffixes in the sense of state (bhāva), occur in the neuter gender. Words ending in tave, etc., and those ending in the kkhattu suffix, are called indeclinables (avyaya).
10:
## Kārakanidessa

47. In whatever sense, such as the object (kamma), where the four great denoters—the verbal inflection (ākhyāta), primary derivative (kita), compound (samāsa), and secondary derivative (taddhita)—are not prescribed (not expressed), that sense is called unexpressed (anutta). In that unexpressed sense of the object, etc., the accusative (dutiyā) and other case endings occur as appropriate.

48. The accusative (dutiyā) case occurs in the sense of the object (kamma) reached by the action (possessing pervasive power). It also occurs in the sense of a moment of time (khaṇa) or a distance of space (addhāna) that is continuously associated with a substance, quality, or action. The accusative case also occurs in association with words called kammapavacanīya such as anu, with words ending in the suffixes ena and to, and with words such as ubhaya.

49. The relation (kāraka) that is independent in accomplishing an action is called the agent (kattukāraka). The relation that is the most effective means (sādhakatama) of accomplishment is called the instrument (karaṇakāraka). The instrumental (tatiyā) case occurs in these agent and instrument relations, in the sense of cause (hetu), in the sense of the locative (sattamī), in the sense of characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa), in the sense of attribute (visesana), in association with saha, and in association with words such as pubba.

50. When wealth is well-given to someone, whether by a junior out of a desire to worship or by a senior out of a desire to favor, the person who gains ownership of that wealth is called the recipient (sampadāna). The dative (catutthī) case occurs in that sense of the recipient and in association with words such as namo.
11:
51. The relation (kāraka) that defines the limit of an action is called the ablative (apādāna); the ablative (pañcamī) case occurs in that sense. The relation which is the location of the agent and the object, which are the supports of the action, is called the locus (okāsa).

52. The locative (sattamī) case occurs in that sense of locus, and in the characteristic action (lakkhaṇakriyā) which marks another action. It also occurs in the object of the root i and the suffix ta following a stem (pakati), and in the object of roots such as gaha.

53. The locative (sattamī) case occurs in the sense of time (kāla), the sense of a sign (nimitta), and the sense of cause (kāraṇa) of roots such as piṇḍacara. That locative case also occurs when associated with the word adhi in the sense of lordship (sāmya), and when associated with the word upa in the sense of excess or superiority (adhika).

54. The mutual dependence of the attribute (visesana) and the substantive (visesya) is called relation (sambandha); the genitive (chaṭṭhī) case occurs in that sense. It also occurs in the sense of the object (kamma) and the agent (kattar) when associated with a primary derivative (kita) suffix.

55. When both the object and the agent are present [in the same sentence], the genitive (chaṭṭhī) does not occur in the sense of the agent. However, in the sense of the suffixes ṇvu, yu, and ti, the genitive occurs optionally in the agent. When associated with the feminine suffixes a and ṇu, the genitive occurs in both the object and the agent. When associated with a kicca suffix, it does not occur in both, or it occurs optionally in the agent only. When associated with suffixes such as niṭṭhā, the genitive definitely does not occur [in both]. In the agent of the ta suffix in the sense of state (bhāva), however, the genitive occurs optionally.
12: 56. The Genitive case (saṭṭhī vibhatti) is optionally applied in the sense of the object (kamma) for the root dis ending in the anta suffix, for the root karu in the sense of making an effort, for the root haru in the sense of imitation, and for the root sati in the sense of remembrance and roots in the sense of harming (hiṃsa). 57. The Genitive case is optionally applied in the sense of the object for the root daya, for the root isu, and in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) for roots in the sense of contentment. However, the Genitive case is always applied in the sense of the object and the agent (kattā) for the suffix ta when it occurs in the sense of the locus (ādhāra/adhikaraṇa). 58. The Locative (sattamī) and Genitive cases are applied in the sense of disregard (anādara). Similarly, in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa), the Locative and Genitive cases are applied. Due to connection with the indeclinables puthu and nānā, the Instrumental (tatiyā) and Ablative (pañcamī) cases are also applied. 59. In connection with the indeclinable rite, the Accusative (dutiyā) and that Ablative case are applied. In connection with the indeclinables vinā and aññatra, the Accusative, Instrumental, and Ablative cases are also applied. In connection with words expressing cause, the Genitive case is applied to a pure noun in the causal sense (hetu). 60. From a pronoun (sabbanāma), all case endings can indeed be applied in the causal sense. The causes for the completion of an action are called kāraka, such as kamma, etc., categorized into secondary (goṇa/apadhāna) and primary (mukha/padhāna). ## End of the Exposition of Kāraka. 58. The state of having a non-distinct meaning (ekatthībhāva) between the qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesya) is called Samāsa (compound). In such cases of non-distinct meaning, Taddhita (derivative) is also prescribed.
13: ## Exposition of Samāsa 61. The state of having a non-distinct meaning (ekatthībhāva) between the qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesya) is called Samāsa. In such cases of non-distinct meaning, Taddhita is also prescribed. 62. A Samāsa where words ending in cases starting from the Accusative (dutiyā) are joined with subsequent nouns is called Tappurisa. In this Tappurisa compound, the qualified word (visesya) usually stands at the end. 63. A Samāsa where a qualifier (visesana) is joined with a qualified (visesya), and if those two together have a unified meaning, it is called Kammadhāraya. In this Kammadhāraya compound, the qualifier usually stands at the beginning. 64. A Samāsa where words expressing numbers are joined with words expressing the thing to be numbered (saṅkheyya), in the sense of a Taddhita suffix, or in the sense of a collective (samāhāra), or when followed by another word, is called Digu. 65. Both Kammadhāraya and Digu compounds are also called Tappurisa. Therefore, if there is a rule applicable to Tappurisa in those two compounds, the wise who understands examples and rules should note that rule.
14: 66. A Samāsa where many words are joined to express the meaning of another word is called Bahubbīhi. It is also called Bahubbīhi when words of similar form (sarūpa) are joined in the sense of fighting (war), or when words for directions are joined in the sense of intermediate directions (vidisā). 67. In that Bahubbīhi compound, the qualifier (visesana), words ending in the Locative (sattamyanta), and words ending in the ta suffix (niṭṭhanta) stand at the beginning. However, when joined with words meaning weapons (āvudha), the Locative-ended word stands at the end. In words like āhita, etc., the niṭṭhanta word optionally stands at the end. 68. The combination of nouns in the sense of a collective (samāhāra) or in the sense of mutual connection (itaretarayoga/asamāhāra) is called Dvanda. In that Dvanda compound, the honored (noble) word and the word with fewer vowels usually stand at the beginning. 69. When indeclinables (avyaya) are joined in the sense of case endings, etc., that compound is desired as Avyayībhāva. Words like pari, etc., are joined with words ending in the Ablative (pañcamī), and words like oraṃ, etc., are joined with words ending in the Genitive (saṭṭhī). 70. In a Saṭṭhī-Tappurisa compound, the word sabhā occurring after words meaning 'king' or 'non-human' (ogre, deity, etc.) becomes neuter gender in the sense of a house, monastery, hall, pavilion, or celestial mansion. The word chāyā preceded by a word expressing a multitude also occurs in the neuter gender. 71. The words senā, surā, sālā, nisā, and chāyā are optionally neuter. However, when clearly indicating the beginning of the meaning of the associated word, the words upajña and upakkama are always neuter.

## Exposition of Taddhita

72. Taddhita suffixes are said to be applied in the sense of relation, in the sense of the kāraka (case-role), in the sense of a collection, in the sense of a state, in the sense of lineage, and in other senses as well. There are also taddhita suffixes that occur at the end of compounds, as well as those known as indeclinables.

## The Kaccāyanasāra is concluded.
